blocks.path: Stye
s: A stye is a small, painful lump on the eyelid.
They're common and should go away within a week.
Styes are rarely a sign of anything serious, but may be painful until they heal.

blocks.path: Stye > Symptoms of a stye
s: A stye usually only affects 1 eye, but it's possible to have more than 1 at a time and on both eyes.

blocks.path: Stye > Symptoms of a stye
s: It's probably not a stye if:

blocks.path: Stye > Symptoms of a stye
s: there's no lump – if your eye or eyelid is swollen, red and watery it's more likely to be conjunctivitis or blepharitis

blocks.path: Stye > Symptoms of a stye
s: the lump is hard but not very painful – this is more likely to be a chalazion

blocks.path: Stye > Symptoms of a stye
s: Find out more about chalazions on the Moorfields Eye Hospital website

blocks.path: Stye > How you can treat a stye yourself
s: To reduce swelling and help the stye heal:

blocks.path: Stye > How you can treat a stye yourself
s: Soak a clean flannel in warm water.

blocks.path: Stye > How you can treat a stye yourself
s: Hold it against your eye for 5 to 10 minutes.

blocks.path: Stye > How you can treat a stye yourself
s: Repeat this 2 to 4 times a day.

blocks.path: Stye > How you can treat a stye yourself
s: To relieve the pain, take painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
Do not give aspirin to children under 16.

blocks.path: Stye > How you can treat a stye yourself
s: Avoid wearing contact lenses and eye make-up until the stye has burst and healed.

blocks.path: Stye > How you can treat a stye yourself > Important: Do not burst a stye
s: Do not try to burst a stye or remove an eyelash yourself.
This can spread the infection.

blocks.path: Stye > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
s: a stye does not get better within a few weeks

blocks.path: Stye > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
s: a stye is very painful or swollen

blocks.path: Stye > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
s: it affects your vision

blocks.path: Stye > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
s: your eye is producing pus

blocks.path: Stye > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
s: the infection has spread to your eye or eyelid

blocks.path: Stye > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
s: You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

blocks.path: Stye > Treatment from a GP
s: If you have a stye, the GP may:

blocks.path: Stye > Treatment from a GP
s: burst the stye with a thin, sterilised needle

blocks.path: Stye > Treatment from a GP
s: remove the eyelash closest to the stye

blocks.path: Stye > Treatment from a GP
s: refer you to an eye specialist in hospital

blocks.path: Stye > How to prevent a stye
s: You can help avoid stye by keeping your eyes clean.

blocks.path: Stye > How to prevent a stye
s: Styes are often caused by bacteria infecting an eyelash follicle or eyelid gland.

blocks.path: Stye > How to prevent a stye
s: You're also more likely to get a stye if you have long-term blepharitis or rosacea.

blocks.path: Stye > How to prevent a stye > Do wash your face and remove eye make-up before bed keep your eyelids and eyelashes clean, especially if you have blepharitis wash your hands before putting contact lenses in or taking them out Don’t
s: do not share towels or flannels with someone who has a stye

blocks.path: Stye > How to prevent a stye > Do wash your face and remove eye make-up before bed keep your eyelids and eyelashes clean, especially if you have blepharitis wash your hands before putting contact lenses in or taking them out Don’t
s: do not rub your eyes if you have not recently washed your hands
